Kennedy Book Award was founded in 1980, with the proceeds from [Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schlesinger,_Jr. "Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.")'s biography, _Robert Kennedy and His Times_. Each year, the organization presents an award to the book which "most faithfully and forcefully reflects Robert Kennedy's purposes – his concern for the poor and the powerless, his struggle for honest and even-handed justice, his conviction that a decent society must assure all young people a fair chance, and his faith that a free democracy can act to remedy disparities of power and opportunity."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights#cite_note-25)_[better source needed_]
Past winners have been:[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Human_Rights#cite_note-26)

Former President Barack Obama was honored with the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Ripple of Hope Award during the foundation’s gala in midtown Manhattan earlier this week.
“I’m not sure if you’ve heard, but I’ve been on this hope kick for a while now. Even ran a couple of campaigns on it. Thank you for officially validating my hope credentials,” Obama said during his acceptance speech.
Kerry Kennedy, RFK’s daughter and the organization’s president, presented Obama with the award, which celebrates leaders “who have demonstrated a commitment to social change.”
“If we summon our best selves, we can inspire others to do the same. It’s easy to succumb to cynicism, the notion that hope is a fool’s game,” Obama said, “When our leaders are content on making up whatever facts they want, a lot of people have begun to doubt the notion of common ground,” Obama said. “Bobby Kennedy’s life reminds us to reject such cynicism.”
Also honored with Ripple of Hope Awards this year were New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy, Discovery President and CEO David Zaslav and Humana CEO Bruce Broussard. Speakers last night included actors Keegan-Michael Key, Alfre Woodard, Alec Baldwin, and journalist Tom Brokaw.

As head of the SACC, Tutu's time was dominated by fundraising for the organisation's projects.[154] Under Tutu's tenure, it was revealed that one of the SACC's divisional directors had been stealing funds. In 1981 a government commission launched to investigate the issue, headed by the judge C. F. Eloff.[155] Tutu gave evidence to the commission, during which he condemned apartheid as "evil" and "unchristian".[156] When the Eloff report was published, Tutu criticised it, focusing particularly on the absence of any theologians on its board, likening it to "a group of blind men" judging the Chelsea Flower Show.[157] In 1981 Tutu also became the rector of St Augustine's Church in Soweto's Orlando West.[158] The following year he published a collection of his sermons and speeches, Crying in the Wilderness: The Struggle for Justice in South Africa;[159] another volume, Hope and Suffering, appeared in 1984.[159]
Activism and the Nobel Peace Prizeedit
Tutu testified on behalf of a captured cell of Umkhonto we Sizwe, an armed anti-apartheid group linked to the banned African National Congress (ANC). He stated that although he was committed to non-violence and censured all who used violence, he could understand why black Africans became violent when their non-violent tactics had failed to overturn apartheid.[160] In an earlier address, he had opined that an armed struggle against South Africa's government had little chance of succeeding but also accused Western nations of hypocrisy for condemning armed liberation groups in southern Africa while they had praised similar organisations in Europe during the Second World War.[161] Tutu also signed a petition calling for the release of ANC activist Nelson Mandela,[162] leading to a correspondence between the pair.[163]
US President Ronald Reagan meeting with Desmond Tutu in 1984. Tutu described Reagan's administration as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks",[164] and Reagan himself as "a racist pure and simple".[165]

After Tutu told journalists that he supported an international economic boycott of South Africa, he was reprimanded before government ministers in October 1979.[166] In March 1980, the government confiscated his passport; this raised his international profile.[167] In 1980, the SACC committed itself to supporting civil disobedience against apartheid.[168] After Thorne was arrested in May, Tutu and Joe Wing led a protest march during which they were arrested, imprisoned overnight, and fined.[169] In the aftermath, a meeting was organised between 20 church leaders including Tutu, Prime Minister P. W. Botha, and seven government ministers. At this August meeting the clerical leaders unsuccessfully urged the government to end apartheid.[170] Although some clergy saw this dialogue as pointless, Tutu disagreed, commenting: "Moses went to Pharaoh repeatedly to secure the release of the Israelites."[171]
In January 1981, the government returned Tutu's passport.[172] In March, he embarked on a five-week tour of Europe and North America, meeting politicians including the UN Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim, and addressing the UN Special Committee Against Apartheid.[173] In England, he met Robert Runcie and gave a sermon in Westminster Abbey, while in Rome he met Pope John Paul II.[174] On his return to South Africa, Botha again ordered Tutu's passport confiscated, preventing him from personally collecting several further honorary degrees.[175] It was returned 17 months later.[176] In September 1982 Tutu addressed the Triennial Convention of the Episcopal Church in New Orleans before traveling to Kentucky to see his daughter Naomi, who lived there with her American husband.[177] Tutu gained a popular following in the US, where he was often compared to civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., although white conservatives like Pat Buchanan and Jerry Falwell lambasted him as an alleged communist sympathiser.[178]

This award is for mothers, who sit at railway stations to try to eke out an existence, selling potatoes, selling mealies, selling produce. This award is for you, fathers, sitting in a single-sex hostel, separated from your children for 11 months a year... This award is for you, mothers in the KTC squatter camp, whose shelters are destroyed callously every day, and who sit on soaking mattresses in the winter rain, holding whimpering babies... This award is for you, the 3.5 million of our people who have been uprooted and dumped as if you were rubbish. This award is for you.
— Desmond Tutu's speech on receiving the Nobel Peace Prize[179]
By the 1980s, Tutu was an icon for many black South Africans, a status rivalled only by Mandela.[180] In August 1983, he became a patron of the new anti-apartheid United Democratic Front (UDF).[181] Tutu angered much of South Africa's press and white minority,[182] especially apartheid supporters.[182] Pro-government media like The Citizen and the South African Broadcasting Corporation criticised him,[183] often focusing on how his middle-class lifestyle contrasted with the poverty of the blacks he claimed to represent.[184] He received hate mail and death threats from white far-right groups like the Wit Wolwe.[185] Although he remained close with prominent white liberals like Helen Suzman,[186] his angry anti-government rhetoric also alienated many white liberals like Alan Paton and Bill Burnett, who believed that apartheid could be gradually reformed away.[187]

In 1984, Tutu embarked on a three-month sabbatical at the General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church in New York.[188] In the city, he was invited to address the United Nations Security Council,[189] later meeting the Congressional Black Caucus and the subcommittees on Africa in the House of Representatives and the Senate.[190] He was also invited to the White House, where he unsuccessfully urged President Ronald Reagan to change his approach to South Africa.[191] He was troubled that Reagan had a warmer relationship with South Africa's government than his predecessor Jimmy Carter, describing Reagan's government as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks".[192] Tutu later called Reagan "a racist pure and simple".[165]
In New York City, Tutu was informed that he had won the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize; he had previously been nominated in 1981, 1982, and 1983.[193] The Nobel Prize selection committee had wanted to recognise a South African and thought Tutu would be a less controversial choice than Mandela or Mangosuthu Buthelezi.[194] In December, he attended the award ceremony in Oslo—which was hampered by a bomb scare—before returning home via Sweden, Denmark, Canada, Tanzania, and Zambia.[195] He shared the US$192,000 prize money with his family, SACC staff, and a scholarship fund for South Africans in exile.[196] He was the second South African to receive the award, after Albert Luthuli in 1960.[164] South Africa's government and mainstream media either downplayed or criticised the award,[197] while the Organisation of African Unity hailed it as evidence of apartheid's impending demise.[198]
Bishop of Johannesburg: 1985–1986edit

After Timothy Bavin retired as Bishop of Johannesburg, Tutu was among five replacement candidates. An elective assembly met at St Barnabas' College in October 1984 and although Tutu was one of the two most popular candidates, the white laity voting bloc consistently voted against his candidature. To break deadlock, a bishops' synod met and decided to appoint Tutu.[199] Black Anglicans celebrated, although many white Anglicans were angry;[200] some withdrew their diocesan quota in protest.[201] Tutu was enthroned as the sixth Bishop of Johannesburg in St Mary's Cathedral in February 1985.[202] The first black man to hold the role,[203] he took over the country's largest diocese, comprising 102 parishes and 300,000 parishioners, approximately 80% of whom were black.[204] In his inaugural sermon, Tutu called on the international community to introduce economic sanctions against South Africa unless apartheid was not being dismantled within 18 to 24 months.[205] He sought to reassure white South Africans that he was not the "horrid ogre" some feared; as bishop he spent much time wooing the support of white Anglicans in his diocese,[206] and resigned as patron of the UDF.[207]
I have no hope of real change from this government unless they are forced. We face a catastrophe in this land and only the action of the international community by applying pressure can save us. Our children are dying. Our land is bleeding and burning and so I call the international community to apply punitive sanctions against this government to help us establish a new South Africa – non-racial, democratic, participatory and just. This is a non-violent strategy to help us do so. There is a great deal of goodwill still in our country between the races. Let us not be so wanton in destroying it. We can live together as one people, one family, black and white together.
— Desmond Tutu, 1985[208]

The mid-1980s saw growing clashes between black youths and the security services; Tutu was invited to speak at many of the funerals of those youths killed.[209] At a Duduza funeral, he intervened to stop the crowd from killing a black man accused of being a government informant.[210] Tutu angered some black South Africans by speaking against the torture and killing of suspected collaborators.[211] For these militants, Tutu's calls for non-violence were perceived as an obstacle to revolution.[212] When Tutu accompanied the US politician Ted Kennedy on the latter's visit to South Africa in January 1985, he was angered that protesters from the Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO)—who regarded Kennedy as an agent of capitalism and American imperialism—disrupted proceedings.[213]
Amid the violence, the ANC called on supporters to make South Africa "ungovernable";[214] foreign companies increasingly disinvested in the country and the South African rand reached a record low.[215] In July 1985, Botha declared a state of emergency in 36 magisterial districts, suspending civil liberties and giving the security services additional powers;[216] he rebuffed Tutu's offer to serve as a go-between for the government and leading black organisations.[217] Tutu continued protesting; in April 1985, he led a small march of clergy through Johannesburg to protest the arrest of Geoff Moselane.[218] In October 1985, he backed the National Initiative for Reconciliation's proposal for people to refrain from work for a day of prayer, fasting, and mourning.[219] He also proposed a national strike against apartheid, angering trade unions whom he had not consulted beforehand.[220]

Tutu continued promoting his cause abroad. In May 1985 he embarked on a speaking tour of the United States,[221] and in October 1985 addressed the political committee of the United Nations General Assembly, urging the international community to impose sanctions on South Africa if apartheid was not dismantled within six months.[222] Proceeding to the United Kingdom, he met with Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.[223] He also formed a Bishop Tutu Scholarship Fund to financially assist South African students living in exile.[224] He returned to the US in May 1986,[91] and in August 1986 visited Japan, China, and Jamaica to promote sanctions.[225] Given that most senior anti-apartheid activists were imprisoned, Mandela referred to Tutu as "public enemy number one for the powers that be".[226]
Archbishop of Cape Town: 1986–1994edit  
Tutu on a visit to San Francisco in 1986
After Philip Russell announced his retirement as the Archbishop of Cape Town,[227] in February 1986 the Black Solidarity Group formed a plan to get Tutu appointed as his replacement.[228] At the time of the meeting, Tutu was in Atlanta, Georgia, receiving the Martin Luther King, Jr. Nonviolent Peace Prize.[229] Tutu secured a two-thirds majority from both the clergy and laity and was then ratified in a unanimous vote by the synod of bishops.[230] He was the first black man to hold the post.[227] Some white Anglicans left the church in protest.[231] More than 1,300 people attended his enthronement ceremony at the Cathedral of St George the Martyr on 7 September 1986.[232] After the ceremony, Tutu held an open-air Eucharist for 10,000 people at the Cape Showgrounds in Goodwood, where he invited Albertina Sisulu and Allan Boesak to give political speeches.[233]

US President Ronald Reagan meeting with Desmond Tutu in 1984. Tutu described Reagan's administration as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks",[164] and Reagan himself as "a racist pure and simple".[165]

After Tutu told journalists that he supported an international economic boycott of South Africa, he was reprimanded before government ministers in October 1979.[166] In March 1980, the government confiscated his passport; this raised his international profile.[167] In 1980, the SACC committed itself to supporting civil disobedience against apartheid.[168] After Thorne was arrested in May, Tutu and Joe Wing led a protest march during which they were arrested, imprisoned overnight, and fined.[169] In the aftermath, a meeting was organised between 20 church leaders including Tutu, Prime Minister P. W. Botha, and seven government ministers. At this August meeting the clerical leaders unsuccessfully urged the government to end apartheid.[170] Although some clergy saw this dialogue as pointless, Tutu disagreed, commenting: "Moses went to Pharaoh repeatedly to secure the release of the Israelites."[171]
In January 1981, the government returned Tutu's passport.[172] In March, he embarked on a five-week tour of Europe and North America, meeting politicians including the UN Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim, and addressing the UN Special Committee Against Apartheid.[173] In England, he met Robert Runcie and gave a sermon in Westminster Abbey, while in Rome he met Pope John Paul II.[174] On his return to South Africa, Botha again ordered Tutu's passport confiscated, preventing him from personally collecting several further honorary degrees.[175] It was returned 17 months later.[176] In September 1982 Tutu addressed the Triennial Convention of the Episcopal Church in New Orleans before traveling to Kentucky to see his daughter Naomi, who lived there with her American husband.[177] Tutu gained a popular following in the US, where he was often compared to civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., although white conservatives like Pat Buchanan and Jerry Falwell lambasted him as an alleged communist sympathiser.[178]

This award is for mothers, who sit at railway stations to try to eke out an existence, selling potatoes, selling mealies, selling produce. This award is for you, fathers, sitting in a single-sex hostel, separated from your children for 11 months a year... This award is for you, mothers in the KTC squatter camp, whose shelters are destroyed callously every day, and who sit on soaking mattresses in the winter rain, holding whimpering babies... This award is for you, the 3.5 million of our people who have been uprooted and dumped as if you were rubbish. This award is for you.
— Desmond Tutu's speech on receiving the Nobel Peace Prize[179]
By the 1980s, Tutu was an icon for many black South Africans, a status rivalled only by Mandela.[180] In August 1983, he became a patron of the new anti-apartheid United Democratic Front (UDF).[181] Tutu angered much of South Africa's press and white minority,[182] especially apartheid supporters.[182] Pro-government media like The Citizen and the South African Broadcasting Corporation criticised him,[183] often focusing on how his middle-class lifestyle contrasted with the poverty of the blacks he claimed to represent.[184] He received hate mail and death threats from white far-right groups like the Wit Wolwe.[185] Although he remained close with prominent white liberals like Helen Suzman,[186] his angry anti-government rhetoric also alienated many white liberals like Alan Paton and Bill Burnett, who believed that apartheid could be gradually reformed away.[187]

In 1984, Tutu embarked on a three-month sabbatical at the General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church in New York.[188] In the city, he was invited to address the United Nations Security Council,[189] later meeting the Congressional Black Caucus and the subcommittees on Africa in the House of Representatives and the Senate.[190] He was also invited to the White House, where he unsuccessfully urged President Ronald Reagan to change his approach to South Africa.[191] He was troubled that Reagan had a warmer relationship with South Africa's government than his predecessor Jimmy Carter, describing Reagan's government as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks".[192] Tutu later called Reagan "a racist pure and simple".[165]
In New York City, Tutu was informed that he had won the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize; he had previously been nominated in 1981, 1982, and 1983.[193] The Nobel Prize selection committee had wanted to recognise a South African and thought Tutu would be a less controversial choice than Mandela or Mangosuthu Buthelezi.[194] In December, he attended the award ceremony in Oslo—which was hampered by a bomb scare—before returning home via Sweden, Denmark, Canada, Tanzania, and Zambia.[195] He shared the US$192,000 prize money with his family, SACC staff, and a scholarship fund for South Africans in exile.[196] He was the second South African to receive the award, after Albert Luthuli in 1960.[164] South Africa's government and mainstream media either downplayed or criticised the award,[197] while the Organisation of African Unity hailed it as evidence of apartheid's impending demise.[198]
Bishop of Johannesburg: 1985–1986edit

After Timothy Bavin retired as Bishop of Johannesburg, Tutu was among five replacement candidates. An elective assembly met at St Barnabas' College in October 1984 and although Tutu was one of the two most popular candidates, the white laity voting bloc consistently voted against his candidature. To break deadlock, a bishops' synod met and decided to appoint Tutu.[199] Black Anglicans celebrated, although many white Anglicans were angry;[200] some withdrew their diocesan quota in protest.[201] Tutu was enthroned as the sixth Bishop of Johannesburg in St Mary's Cathedral in February 1985.[202] The first black man to hold the role,[203] he took over the country's largest diocese, comprising 102 parishes and 300,000 parishioners, approximately 80% of whom were black.[204] In his inaugural sermon, Tutu called on the international community to introduce economic sanctions against South Africa unless apartheid was not being dismantled within 18 to 24 months.[205] He sought to reassure white South Africans that he was not the "horrid ogre" some feared; as bishop he spent much time wooing the support of white Anglicans in his diocese,[206] and resigned as patron of the UDF.[207]
I have no hope of real change from this government unless they are forced. We face a catastrophe in this land and only the action of the international community by applying pressure can save us. Our children are dying. Our land is bleeding and burning and so I call the international community to apply punitive sanctions against this government to help us establish a new South Africa – non-racial, democratic, participatory and just. This is a non-violent strategy to help us do so. There is a great deal of goodwill still in our country between the races. Let us not be so wanton in destroying it. We can live together as one people, one family, black and white together.
— Desmond Tutu, 1985[208]

The mid-1980s saw growing clashes between black youths and the security services; Tutu was invited to speak at many of the funerals of those youths killed.[209] At a Duduza funeral, he intervened to stop the crowd from killing a black man accused of being a government informant.[210] Tutu angered some black South Africans by speaking against the torture and killing of suspected collaborators.[211] For these militants, Tutu's calls for non-violence were perceived as an obstacle to revolution.[212] When Tutu accompanied the US politician Ted Kennedy on the latter's visit to South Africa in January 1985, he was angered that protesters from the Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO)—who regarded Kennedy as an agent of capitalism and American imperialism—disrupted proceedings.[213]
Amid the violence, the ANC called on supporters to make South Africa "ungovernable";[214] foreign companies increasingly disinvested in the country and the South African rand reached a record low.[215] In July 1985, Botha declared a state of emergency in 36 magisterial districts, suspending civil liberties and giving the security services additional powers;[216] he rebuffed Tutu's offer to serve as a go-between for the government and leading black organisations.[217] Tutu continued protesting; in April 1985, he led a small march of clergy through Johannesburg to protest the arrest of Geoff Moselane.[218] In October 1985, he backed the National Initiative for Reconciliation's proposal for people to refrain from work for a day of prayer, fasting, and mourning.[219] He also proposed a national strike against apartheid, angering trade unions whom he had not consulted beforehand.[220]

Tutu continued promoting his cause abroad. In May 1985 he embarked on a speaking tour of the United States,[221] and in October 1985 addressed the political committee of the United Nations General Assembly, urging the international community to impose sanctions on South Africa if apartheid was not dismantled within six months.[222] Proceeding to the United Kingdom, he met with Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.[223] He also formed a Bishop Tutu Scholarship Fund to financially assist South African students living in exile.[224] He returned to the US in May 1986,[91] and in August 1986 visited Japan, China, and Jamaica to promote sanctions.[225] Given that most senior anti-apartheid activists were imprisoned, Mandela referred to Tutu as "public enemy number one for the powers that be".[226]
Archbishop of Cape Town: 1986–1994edit  
Tutu on a visit to San Francisco in 1986
After Philip Russell announced his retirement as the Archbishop of Cape Town,[227] in February 1986 the Black Solidarity Group formed a plan to get Tutu appointed as his replacement.[228] At the time of the meeting, Tutu was in Atlanta, Georgia, receiving the Martin Luther King, Jr. Nonviolent Peace Prize.[229] Tutu secured a two-thirds majority from both the clergy and laity and was then ratified in a unanimous vote by the synod of bishops.[230] He was the first black man to hold the post.[227] Some white Anglicans left the church in protest.[231] More than 1,300 people attended his enthronement ceremony at the Cathedral of St George the Martyr on 7 September 1986.[232] After the ceremony, Tutu held an open-air Eucharist for 10,000 people at the Cape Showgrounds in Goodwood, where he invited Albertina Sisulu and Allan Boesak to give political speeches.[233]
